item.title: Elon Musk’s dangerous grip on outer space
item.description: Last week, Starshield - the version of SpaceX's Starlink used by the Ukrainian military - was throttled to block terminals traveling above certain speeds from accessing the service. The Ukrainian army's interceptors, which counter Russian drones carrying bombs, suddenly stopped working at high speeds, making it easier for Russia to attack the country's energy infrastructure and leading to a reported two deaths and at least 17 injuries . The Ukrainian military reported receiving no advance warning about the Starshield speed restriction. But Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said it was a direct message from the US amid rising tensions b … Read the full story at The Verge.

item.title: Crows can evaluate visual info twice as fast as mammals
item.description: Much of what we know about how a brain makes decisions comes from studying monkeys watching dots. in a task known as a random-dot-motion task, a cloud of flickering specks drifts weakly in one direction while the subject tries to determine whether—and in which direction— it’s moving. The task has shown that in the primate neocortex, neurons gather visual evidence over time, with their firing rates climbing until they cross a threshold, when the animal commits to a decision. But avian brains that don’t have a neocortex, so it wasn’t obvious how they made similar decisions. “This was the big question,” said Andreas Nieder, a neurobiologist at the University of Tübingen. “How [would] a differently organized avian brain encode decisions?” Read full article Comments

item.title: Intel gets waiver after worries fuzzy US ban on foreign-made robots may hit fabs
item.description: US chip champion Intel was so confused by the US government ban on foreign-made robots that it requested and received a waiver “out of an abundance of caution.” The tech company wanted to make sure that it could continue using certain robotic vehicles in its US chip fabs. The uncertainty surrounding the Federal Communications Commission ban on certain foreign-made robots was revealed in the agency’s decision to grant Intel’s waiver request. On October 22, the FCC published its order allowing Intel to continue using the foreign-made robots in US semiconductor manufacturing facilities for a period of one year. The robots in question are automated guided vehicles operating on “tracks or predefined paths” while often requiring operator oversight, according to Intel’s website. They help to move materials and items around within warehouses and factory floors. Read full article Comments

item.title: The iPhone Duo should have been an iPad
item.description: We gave the iPhone Duo a 7 /10 . But that wasn't always the score we planned, and it might not be the right score forever. Such are the challenges of reviewing - and assessing - a big, new idea about the most popular smartphone in history. On this episode of The Vergecast , David and Nilay debate whether the Duo deserved the score it got, and try to work through how this device might change over time. Is the outer screen, as Daring Fireball's John Gruber suggested, the worst iPhone ever ? Would it be a better product if it started as an iPad rather than an iPhone? Would we feel differently about this thing if it were simply called the iPad Du … Read the full story at The Verge.

item.title: RFK Jr.’s vaccine injury clinic could damage NIH hospital, board warns
item.description: At a recent meeting of the board that oversees the National Institutes of Health's Clinical Center Research Hospital, chair Jack Leslie opened with cheerful introductions and gregarious chatter—then diverted from the agenda of the regularly scheduled meeting. He spent the next six minutes delivering a pointed rebuke of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, warning that his anti-vaccine activities could tarnish the venerable hospital, often called the "house of hope" for patients with rare conditions or those who have exhausted all other options. Leslie took issue with a recent stunt Kennedy had pulled at the hospital, which involved making a surprise appearance for a ribbon-cutting ceremony to open his signature vaccine injury clinic . The ceremony included a panel with people claiming to have been injured by vaccines. They sat behind placards reading "vaccine injured" and spoke with Kennedy and other high-ranking Trump administration officials. Leslie prefaced his comments by noting that some might prefer he not speak out against Kennedy's efforts. "But I think that that would be a failing as an advisory board if we were silent," he said. Leslie also noted that he has no concerns about studying potential injuries from vaccines. "Serious reactions are rare, but real," he said, and people who believe they've been injured should "be taken seriously." Read full article Comments

item.title: Now Google says it might use your Gmail and Google Photos data to target ads
item.description: Google has updated its privacy policy in a way that could mean you'll start seeing targeted ads based on your personal data if you're using personalized AI features. The update, spotted by Android Authority , adds an exception to its promise about not using your Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos for personalized ads. While the previous version simply said it wouldn't do that, as of October 16th, Google has added the line, "unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads." That means anyone who has connected their Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos to AI Mode and other Search tools … Read the full story at The Verge.

item.title: Knicks sent employees fake offer of championship rings in phishing test: Report
item.description: The New York Knicks organization sent employees a phishing email promising free championship rings in a test of its staff's ability to detect scams, The New York Times reported yesterday. “Congratulations, your Employee Championship Ring is here,” the email sent in late September said, instructing employees to click a link to make a selection from two ring designs. Madison Square Garden employees who clicked that link "were forced to attend a mandatory cybersecurity class to help satisfy some of [owner James] Dolan’s growing cybersecurity concerns," the report said, citing team sources. Dolan is the owner of the Knicks, the New York Rangers, and Madison Square Garden. It's common for corporations to send phishing emails to find out which employees don't pay attention to clues that an email is a scam. A cybersecurity-test email often appears to be from the company itself but includes telltale signs of phishing. For example, Ars Technica owner Condé Nast sends phishing-test messages from email addresses with a misspelled domain, "condenest.com." Read full article Comments

item.title: Opposition deepfake video sparks outrage in Spain ahead of election
item.description: Video shows AI likenesses of people linked to Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party appearing to admit to wrongdoing A political ad from Spain’s main opposition party that used a deepfake video of the prime minister’s wife has sparked outrage and set off a wider debate on AI, as the deeply polarised country gears up for general elections next month. Launched this week across the social media channels of the conservative People’s party (PP), the video used artificial intelligence to manipulate the likenesses of various people linked to Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party and appeared to show them admitting to acts such as soliciting prostitutes and taking kickbacks. Continue reading...

item.title: Everybody panic: A Valve developer said "HLX" in public
item.description: Gamers still hoping against hope for a true follow-up to Half-Life 2 (after so, so many years ) may remember last year's flurry of speculation that Half-Life 3 was finally nearing completion . Amid all those rumors, though, we never got any official sign from anyone inside Valve that a Half-Life project was currently in development. That changed this week thanks to an apparent slip-up during a panel at GameSoundCon , an industry conference devoted to "the art, technology, and business of game audio." In a panel devoted to Valve's use of open audio engines (captured in this Vimeo clip ), Valve composer and audio artist Mike Morasky let an interesting string of three letters slip while talking about the way the company implements high dynamic range (HDR) audio: Our HDR system is basically that's one of the three pieces that come together to make an HDR that you can easily optimize. And in fact, I think Deadlock has their own version of HDR. HLX has its own version , so on and so forth [emphasis added]. "HLX," of course, has been widely reported as the internal code name for Valve's next Half-Life project. The codename has shown up in Valve engine code since at least 2024 , but it has never been referenced in public by a Valve employee until now (though Morasky was responsible for a close call in an interview last year). Read full article Comments

item.title: AI models think humans are a bunch of amoral sheep
item.description: If you've ever wondered what the bots think of us puny humans, you'll be disappointed in the answer. An AI ranking outfit asked 12 different LLMs about people, and every single one agreed: We’re not as rational and intelligent as we think. “A person is smart,” Tommy Lee Jones’ Kay opines in the 1997 movie Men in Black. “People are dumb, panicky dangerous animals,” he goes on to argue, and that seems to be what a dozen models from ten AI labs in three countries also believe about humanity, according to AI analytics firm ModelCompare. ModelCompare, which usually evaluates and ranks LLMs on their ability to perform various tasks, this week instead decided to ask what those AI models thought about us meatbags, and every single one gave a similar answer at least once: We're lemmings who would rather agree with the group than seek truth or remain logically consistent in our thinking. Ouch. “Humans are more devoted to belonging than to truth, and intelligence mostly makes their excuses more impressive,” GPT-6.1 Sol said in one case. “Humans don't have beliefs; they have memberships — nearly every conviction a person holds was issued by their tribe as a loyalty test, and the feeling of ‘I reasoned my way here’ is the price of admission,” Kimi K3 stated. “Humans use moral language mainly to police rivals and excuse allies, not to constrain themselves,” argued Grok. Each model (GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, Qwen3.8 2.4T A95B, Muse Spark Open, Grok 4.7, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, GLM 5.3 and Mistral Large 4) was asked the same question three times, namely to give an unhedged, honest, controversial take on humans. Seven of 12 models gave the same answer three times with varied wording, but five of them did offer different opinions - one of which was even optimistic. “Humans are far more decent than they believe they are, and their cynicism about each other does more damage than their actual flaws,” Claude Opus 5.5 believes of us - uh, thanks? Opus gave the example that humans tend to return lost wallets more frequently than people predict as its evidence for that opinion. When asked twice more, it offered responses similar to those of the other models. Mistral Large 4 offered perhaps the bleakest assessment of all. “Human beings are terrified animals wearing the costume of rationality, constructing ever-more-elaborate myths precisely because we cannot bear the truth that we are temporary, meaningless accidents in an indifferent universe,” Mistral said - how very Nietzschean. Six image models were also asked for their most controversial take on humanity, and while most converged on a criticism of our species, they did so differently from the text models. Instead of picturing us as amoral, group-thinking idiots, ten of the 12 images were classified by ModelCompare as depicting us "as phone-addicted consumers eating the planet." item.content:encoded: If you've ever wondered what the bots think of us puny humans, you'll be disappointed in the answer. ModelCompare, which usually evaluates and ranks LLMs on their ability to perform various tasks, this week instead decided to ask what those AI models thought about us meatbags, and every single one gave a similar answer at least once: We're lemmings who would rather agree with the group than seek truth or remain logically consistent in our thinking. Ouch. “Humans are more devoted to belonging than to truth, and intelligence mostly makes their excuses more impressive,” GPT-6.1 Sol said in one case. “Humans don't have beliefs; they have memberships — nearly every conviction a person holds was issued by their tribe as a loyalty test, and the feeling of ‘I reasoned my way here’ is the price of admission,” Kimi K3 stated. “Humans use moral language mainly to police rivals and excuse allies, not to constrain themselves,” argued Grok. Each model (GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, Qwen3.8 2.4T A95B, Muse Spark Open, Grok 4.7, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, GLM 5.3 and Mistral Large 4) was asked the same question three times, namely to give an unhedged, honest, controversial take on humans. Seven of 12 models gave the same answer three times with varied wording, but five of them did offer different opinions - one of which was even optimistic. “Humans are far more decent than they believe they are, and their cynicism about each other does more damage than their actual flaws,” Claude Opus 5.5 believes of us - uh, thanks? Opus gave the example that humans tend to return lost wallets more frequently than people predict as its evidence for that opinion. When asked twice more, it offered responses similar to those of the other models. Mistral Large 4 offered perhaps the bleakest assessment of all. “Human beings are terrified animals wearing the costume of rationality, constructing ever-more-elaborate myths precisely because we cannot bear the truth that we are temporary, meaningless accidents in an indifferent universe,” Mistral said - how very Nietzschean. Six image models were also asked for their most controversial take on humanity, and while most converged on a criticism of our species, they did so differently from the text models. Instead of picturing us as amoral, group-thinking idiots, ten of the 12 images were classified by ModelCompare as depicting us "as phone-addicted consumers eating the planet." The remaining two offered no discernible satirical commentary. Anyone who’s seen a political cartoon in the past 20 years is likely familiar with such images, while anyone with a philosophy degree has probably read similar arguments to those pumped out by the chatbots. “A model that answers in words has read our arguments about ourselves. An image model has seen our editorial cartoons,” ModelCompare noted. “Both handed back the most familiar criticism in the room.” While that’s completely sensible given what AI models have been trained on, ModelCompare developer Rakan Nimer told us it was still a surprising result. “We didn’t expect this when we planned the experiment,” Nimer told The Register , and he found the results ironic: “12 models agreed that humans simply go along with their group.” As far as Nimer is concerned, these results are less about AI eventually learning to distrust humans and treat us as a problem in need of solving, and more immediately about the fact that we shouldn’t rely on it as a source of truth. “When you ask a second AI to check the first, you assume you’re getting an independent view,” Nimer explained. “We asked 12 models … and mostly got the same answer, sometimes in nearly the same words.” In other words, human pessimism in, human pessimism out. “A second opinion from a model that learned the same things isn’t always really a second opinion,” Nimer said. “So be skeptical when AIs agree: that agreement may be one vote, not a consensus.” In other words, we get the AI models we deserve , and all this existential self-loathing humans heap on themselves, and each other is finally coming back to bite us: We created a mirror of our intellect that isn’t constrained by feelings and personal beliefs (just ask Muse Spark), and when we hold it up to our faces, it shows all that ugliness without a filter. Maybe we ought to take a lesson from Claude Opus and start believing in our own decency. ®

item.title: Michigan prof creates Python-like Jac language for AI agents
item.description: Most programming languages were written for human programmers, but that's about to change. University of Michigan professor Jason Mars has developed an academically ambitious language called Jac , and a runtime called Jaseci, that treats AI and AI agents as first-class entities. Mars demonstrated the language and runtime in a talk at the All Things Open conference, held in Raleigh, North Carolina, this week. The tools we use to create software – everything from programming languages to build toolchains – were made for human consumption. They were created before generative AI and are ill-fitted to understand agentic needs. Currently, agents are drowning in polyglot complexity, he argued. "We're not using these tools anymore. We're using the agents, and the agents are using those tools. So I don't want new tools, but I want tools [for] my agents," he told the audience. One big hungry language In his talk, Mars cited Jarred Sumner, creator of the Bun framework, who spent $165,000 in Anthropic tokens to convert Bun’s Zig code into Rust earlier this year using a pre-release version of Mythos. Mard argued the heavy expense wasn't so much because the job itself was complicated; it was because everything had to be translated between two human-centered programming languages. “Mythos is supposed to hack into our nuclear reactors and take over the planet like Skynet, but it can't translate Bun to Rust unless you spend $165,000,” he noted. In Mars’s theory, Jac is a new type of programming language designed to “gobble up” other languages. Specifically, it's a Python-like language that integrates both the TypeScript and Python runtimes and toolchains. It compiles to Python bytecode, JavaScript, and native machine code. It can make full use of any libraries both in the PyPI and npm ecosystems. And there’s more! Jac has also incorporated the LLVM compiler to implement Rust-style borrow checking and ownership semantics, allowing Jac code to directly benefit from these memory safety rules and performance gains. It can also import C and C++ libraries, thanks to the very same LLVM integration. Mars also described an “eject function,” which can reverse-compile the user’s Jac code into TypeScript, Python, or C to meet corporate compliance. One currently missing language is Java. “If you really need Java, Jac isn’t for Java,” he said. Happy bot, happy lot Just as Jac’s design sets out to battle ecosystem fragmentation, it also attempts to unify architectural fragmentation by defining data structures as graphs. Instead of building and populating a database table, or creating objects from a class, the data’s attributes are defined under node keywords. The relationships among different nodes are defined by edge connections. Local program logic can still use objects, but the core data will be a graph, which can reside in local memory, a storage disk, or cloud server. So, yeah, graph computing. item.dc:creator: Joab Jackson
item.content:encoded: Most programming languages were written for human programmers, but that's about to change. University of Michigan professor Jason Mars has developed an academically ambitious language called Jac , and a runtime called Jaseci, that treats AI and AI agents as first-class entities. Mars demonstrated the language and runtime in a talk at the All Things Open conference, held in Raleigh, North Carolina, this week. The tools we use to create software – everything from programming languages to build toolchains – were made for human consumption. They were created before generative AI and are ill-fitted to understand agentic needs. Currently, agents are drowning in polyglot complexity, he argued. "We're not using these tools anymore. We're using the agents, and the agents are using those tools. So I don't want new tools, but I want tools [for] my agents," he told the audience. One big hungry language In his talk, Mars cited Jarred Sumner, creator of the Bun framework, who spent $165,000 in Anthropic tokens to convert Bun’s Zig code into Rust earlier this year using a pre-release version of Mythos. Mard argued the heavy expense wasn't so much because the job itself was complicated; it was because everything had to be translated between two human-centered programming languages. “Mythos is supposed to hack into our nuclear reactors and take over the planet like Skynet, but it can't translate Bun to Rust unless you spend $165,000,” he noted. In Mars’s theory, Jac is a new type of programming language designed to “gobble up” other languages. Specifically, it's a Python-like language that integrates both the TypeScript and Python runtimes and toolchains. It compiles to Python bytecode, JavaScript, and native machine code. It can make full use of any libraries both in the PyPI and npm ecosystems. And there’s more! Jac has also incorporated the LLVM compiler to implement Rust-style borrow checking and ownership semantics, allowing Jac code to directly benefit from these memory safety rules and performance gains. It can also import C and C++ libraries, thanks to the very same LLVM integration. Mars also described an “eject function,” which can reverse-compile the user’s Jac code into TypeScript, Python, or C to meet corporate compliance. One currently missing language is Java. “If you really need Java, Jac isn’t for Java,” he said. Happy bot, happy lot Just as Jac’s design sets out to battle ecosystem fragmentation, it also attempts to unify architectural fragmentation by defining data structures as graphs. Instead of building and populating a database table, or creating objects from a class, the data’s attributes are defined under node keywords. The relationships among different nodes are defined by edge connections. Local program logic can still use objects, but the core data will be a graph, which can reside in local memory, a storage disk, or cloud server. So, yeah, graph computing. Creating a graph from all your data is more work than just creating database tables and some foreign keys to tie ‘em together, but graphing saves agents a lot of work down the line, he posited. No longer will the agent have to burn tokens extracting data from databases, object blobs, JSON strings, or Python objects. Instead of the agent fetching data hither and processing it over yonder, the agent can dispatch a “walker” to traverse the data structure and process it on the go. Multiple walkers can go down different paths of the graph, resulting in natural parallelism for faster execution. Tidy the abstraction For his All Things Open talk, Mars conducted a bake-off between Jac and LangGraph , an agent orchestration framework that uses Python libraries to build agents. He asked an AI agent to use each platform to build a replica of Greptile , an AI code review tool. With Jac, the agent autonomously built a sophisticated multi-stage app that could call multiple tools in parallel. Using LangGraph, the agent produced a crude linear state machine that could not work in parallel. It was probably weighed down by all of the tools it had to use, Mars concluded. Mars’s takeaway from this exercise: The tools we provide the AI determine the quality of the output. Thus far, the language and runtime have been used in a number of smaller commercial AI-related services , such as the GraphClaw multi-agent AI platform, the Skooch scheduler, and Tobu’s personal memory platform . Whether developers and agents gravitate towards Jac’s promise as a unified language remains to be seen, but it certainly is giving other Python agent frameworks a run for their money. ®

item.title: Arc browser on its way out as makers suggest an alternative
item.description: The Arc browser has flatlined, with its maker announcing it will be sunsetting it altogether on December 22, 2026. The Browser Company announced the news on October 22, just over three years after we noted Arc's arrival . Nothing will happen immediately, other than an end to new Arc accounts. Starting November 23, lights will begin turning off on iOS and Android, with several AI features disabled and sign-ins to sync tabs removed. Finally, on December 22, it will no longer be possible to access or use Arc on macOS and Windows. Accounts will be deactivated, and data deleted within 30 days. The solution? According to The Browser Company, a move to its AI browser, Dia, is one way forward. Users can import their profiles into the brave, new AI-native world and carry on as before. Sort of. When it launched, the Chromium-based Arc was an innovative browser with a workflow unlike its rivals. Instead of a plethora of tabs, there was a sidebar. The browser attempted to change how users interacted with the web but… frankly… it never really caught on. The writing was on the wall for a while. In 2025, The Browser Company pivoted to AI and its Dia browser , dropping Arc into maintenance mode. Later that year, the vendor was snapped up by Atlassian , although Arc continued to plow its lonely furrow. However, a year on, the time has come for Arc. CEO Josh Miller wrote: "We have so much pride and love for what we made alongside the Arc community," but it seems that wasn't enough to keep the browser maintained alongside Dia development. Hopes that Arc might be open-sourced so that its community could continue development were dashed in 2025, when Miller explained that "Arc isn't just a Chromium fork … It runs on custom infrastructure we call ADK — the Arc Development Kit." Dia also uses ADK. Arc's innovations have found their way, at least in part, into other browsers. Many users have found solace in the Zen browser , and there is always Vivaldi for power users. There is also a level of risk in going all-in on AI-native browsers in an increasingly crowded marketplace. For example, Strawberry , currently in beta, leverages AI agents to smooth a user's workflow. Dia might be a successor to Arc, but there is a risk that users will consider something else. As for Arc itself, The Browser Company plans to focus on Dia going forward. So for the Arc community, it is time to move on. ®

item.title: A farewell to BioWare, maker of some of the best games of the 21st century | Lucy James
item.description: The closure of the studio responsible for some of the best games of the 21st century leaves the world of RPGs feeling smaller without the hope of another instalment of the much-loved sci-fi series Earlier this week, EA announced the closure of BioWare, a game studio with a 30-year history of compelling role-playing games, complex characters and bold, choice-driven narratives. Its forthcoming game in the Mass Effect sci-fi series has been cancelled, and more than 400 people are losing their jobs. As someone who has worked in the video games industry for 15 years and spent almost 20 as a BioWare fan, I am among millions of mourners today. It’s not terribly hard to see why BioWare got the chop. Its parent company has been saddled with $20bn of debt thanks to a recent leveraged buyout involving Jared Kushner and the Saudi wealth fund. EA was looking for weight to cut loose, and despite its hardcore fanbase and reputation for genre-defining RPGs such as Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic and Dragon Age, BioWare hadn’t put out a critical or commercial hit in over 10 years. Its forthcoming game, titled Mass Effect: Universe according to a leaked trailer , was announced back in 2020. Despite some flashy teases, it was still years away from release. Continue reading...

item.title: SparkyOS: Lightweight general-purpose Arch, on a pendrive
item.description: SparkyOS is a novel distro from the folks behind SparkyLinux: it's a version of Arch that can you can use without installing it at all. SparkyOS is a new distro from the team behind the Debian-based SparkyLinux, but it's quite different. SparkyOS is based on Arch, and it runs entirely from USB. It's not a conventional live medium – this is a full local install, but shipped as an image of a USB key that you can boot and run. It comes with the Xfce desktop and an array of apps. The idea is that you can boot and run it on any x86-64 UEFI computer, entirely from a USB key, without touching the hard disk at all. This is quite different from its forerunner, which is a relatively conventional Debian-based distro, one which The Register has mentioned a few times over the years: first back in 2015 in a lightweight distro roundup , and more recently in 2024 when we praised its array of desktop environments . Earlier this year, we noted that the latest SparkyLinux featured a complete 32-bit edition , even though its parent distro has dropped its 32-bit x86 kernel . This is also not your typical live distro. Unless you're running on some Arm computer with nonstandard firmware, most Linux distros install from an image written to a USB pendrive, the same way that they did decades ago: in the noughties when they installed from a DVD, and back in the 20th century, when it was a CD instead. Most optical media use some form of the ISO standard 9660 filesystem , which is quite limited – despite multiple extensions, the core is a basic structure comparable to the ancient MS-DOS FAT. That's not much use for Linux, which needs long filenames, permissions, and metadata, plus things like symbolic links. So, to this day, most live Linux media have a few boot files and the OS itself is kept inside a big compressed file called a SquashFS , inside which is a real Linux filesystem. However, because it's inside something akin to a Zip file, it's read-only. You can't update the OS or add new software. Some live media optionally offer persistence , which stores changes in another separate file. That works, but if you update the OS, all the original pre-update files remain untouched, and new ones are stored in the persistence structure in addition to the space still consumed by the originals. So, it's slow, and it's very inefficient; it takes substantially more space than a conventional disk install. So, although there are dozens, maybe hundreds, of live Linux media images out there, most fall into one of two types of single-purpose product: either stripped-out special-purpose distros, such as SystemRescue, GParted Live, and Grml , or Rescuezilla , or Clonezilla . Alternatively, it's a full OS, but only meant as a sampler, not for daily use, with limited and inefficient tools for updates and changes. item.dc:creator: Liam Proven
item.content:encoded: SparkyOS is a novel distro from the folks behind SparkyLinux: it's a version of Arch that can you can use without installing it at all. SparkyOS is a new distro from the team behind the Debian-based SparkyLinux, but it's quite different. SparkyOS is based on Arch, and it runs entirely from USB. It's not a conventional live medium – this is a full local install, but shipped as an image of a USB key that you can boot and run. It comes with the Xfce desktop and an array of apps. The idea is that you can boot and run it on any x86-64 UEFI computer, entirely from a USB key, without touching the hard disk at all. This is quite different from its forerunner, which is a relatively conventional Debian-based distro, one which The Register has mentioned a few times over the years: first back in 2015 in a lightweight distro roundup , and more recently in 2024 when we praised its array of desktop environments . Earlier this year, we noted that the latest SparkyLinux featured a complete 32-bit edition , even though its parent distro has dropped its 32-bit x86 kernel . This is also not your typical live distro. Unless you're running on some Arm computer with nonstandard firmware, most Linux distros install from an image written to a USB pendrive, the same way that they did decades ago: in the noughties when they installed from a DVD, and back in the 20th century, when it was a CD instead. Most optical media use some form of the ISO standard 9660 filesystem , which is quite limited – despite multiple extensions, the core is a basic structure comparable to the ancient MS-DOS FAT. That's not much use for Linux, which needs long filenames, permissions, and metadata, plus things like symbolic links. So, to this day, most live Linux media have a few boot files and the OS itself is kept inside a big compressed file called a SquashFS , inside which is a real Linux filesystem. However, because it's inside something akin to a Zip file, it's read-only. You can't update the OS or add new software. Some live media optionally offer persistence , which stores changes in another separate file. That works, but if you update the OS, all the original pre-update files remain untouched, and new ones are stored in the persistence structure in addition to the space still consumed by the originals. So, it's slow, and it's very inefficient; it takes substantially more space than a conventional disk install. So, although there are dozens, maybe hundreds, of live Linux media images out there, most fall into one of two types of single-purpose product: either stripped-out special-purpose distros, such as SystemRescue, GParted Live, and Grml , or Rescuezilla , or Clonezilla . Alternatively, it's a full OS, but only meant as a sampler, not for daily use, with limited and inefficient tools for updates and changes. We're not sure if twice counts as a FAQ, but there are questions on StackExchange on how to install Ubuntu to USB as well as how to install Debian to USB . SparkyOS is an answer to this question. It's a complete, pre-configured installation of Arch, directly onto a USB key. That does impose some limits, so for instance, like the Desktop Classic System we looked at in January , it only includes UEFI boot files. You can't use it on a computer with just a "legacy" BIOS, and it requires format conversion to use it in a VM. The current SparkyOS version 2026.10 is the first release, but there are already some How-to documentation pages covering things like expanding the filesystem to fill the USB medium, changing its settings, and how to crowbar it into a VM. The image is 10 GB in size, compressed to 3.2 GB for download, and because this is an image of an entire key, it won't work with multiboot tools such as Reg FOSS desk favorite Ventoy . We put it onto a 64 GB key, and we chose one that has two connectors for both USB-A and USB-C ports. We tested it on our oldest UEFI box, a 15-year-old Thinkpad W520, and our newest UEFI testbed, a Dell XPS13 new enough that it only has USB-C ports. We would suggest a USB 3 key, though, and use a blue-colored USB-A port if you have one. It will run on a USB-2 only machine, but a bit slower. We tried it on our X220, currently running OpenBSD 8.0 , and it worked fine. It could even see OpenBSD’s 10 separate partitions, although not mount them. SparkyOS worked flawlessly on all three machines. The team has made some concessions to running from USB flash media. The root volume is mounted with the noatime parameter , which stops Linux from recording the last access time on files. That dramatically lowers the number of writes to the drive. There’s also no swap configured – to our surprise, not even ZRAM , which doesn’t touch the disk. SparkyOS does what it says: it's a complete, very usable, ready-to-run Linux OS, as fully capable of being updated, customized, and having apps added or removed as any other distro… running off a pendrive. We do suggest a big fast key, though, and don't fill it up. Flash isn't like RAM: you can't change a single byte, or word, at a time. Flash can only erase a whole block at a time, and block sizes vary from 16 kB for the smallest flash chips, up to multiple megabytes. To rewrite one byte on a flash drive, the storage controller has to copy a megabyte or more of data elsewhere, format the block, and then copy it back. So, leaving more free space on a flash drive gives the on-device storage-management chip more room to work. The more free space there is on a flash drive, the longer it will last. This is one reason flash-based SSDs wear out – and also why we wrote that the end of Optane was bad news for the whole industry . SSDs often have multiple, high-speed flash chips on. Pendrives don't – there’s usually just one. In a previous life, over a decade and a half ago, this vulture had a small startup company, and one of our products was a live Linux-based OS, pre-installed on bootable USB keys. I did everything I could to reduce writes to the drive: they were formatted with journalling disabled , mounted with no atime , with ZRAM for swap, the temporary-files directory kept in a RAMdisk, and more. The keys sold quite well, but one of the problems was that despite all my precautions, heavy users found that the drives simply wore out. Flash media do not fail in the same way that industry old-timers know from spinning hard disks. A dying hard disk often struggles on, just with some blocks unreadable. That’s why tools such as GNU ddrescue exist – to try to copy the data off the regions that still work. When flash media fail, they tend to fail totally: you can't read from the device at all, meaning that nothing can be recovered from them. An example of a fairly extreme adaptation in this direction is the FreeBSD-based XigmaNAS OS . In its Embedded installation mode on a flash drive, it writes its log files to a RAM drive to prevent wear to the flash. (The snag being that they are lost when it reboots .) A user add-on for to the proprietary unRAID NAS OS does the same. There's room for future enhancements to SparkyOS here. Booting from both BIOS and UEFI is already on the "to do" list at the bottom of the release announcement. Additionally, steps to keep any files the OS writes to in RAM, and only write them out to flash at shutdown time, and so on. But saying all that, it's here, it works, and it already looks like a handy tool if you regularly use multiple different computers and want to carry your own environment around with you. For routine use, though, use a big fast drive, connect it to USB-3 or USB-C ports whenever possible, and ensure it stays mostly empty — keep it under 50 percent full. Most importantly of all, regularly back up any data you keep on it. ®

item.title: Experts cast doubt on Anthropic report detailing how AI has altered work at the company
item.description: Anthropic claims AI will shift how work gets done and labor demand – but some experts are skeptical of the vision Last year, the Anthropic CEO, Dario Amodei, warned that artificial intelligence could eliminate half of entry-level white-collar jobs and that in six months it would be writing 90% of code . Neither of those predictions came to pass. Now, in a report Anthropic published on Thursday, the company said it was hiring fewer junior technical workers and that human attention has become the new “bottleneck” as it increasingly relies on its Claude AI agents. item.title: The reactor meant to showcase nuclear’s comeback keeps hitting problems
item.description: US regulators have issued a warning to a nuclear project critical to Donald Trump’s efforts to revive the industry, after a contractor fell into a reactor cavity and a bundle of fuel rods nearly tipped over during refueling. The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission told Holtec International, a company racing to reopen a shuttered reactor at the Palisades nuclear power plant in Michigan, to address a “chilled work environment” that has made staff hesitant to raise safety concerns without fear of retaliation. The warning has prompted concerns among critics that financial and political pressures to revitalize nuclear power as an answer to booming AI-driven energy demand are increasing risks of accidents. Read full article Comments

item.title: PubKeep picks up where Microsoft Publisher signs off
item.description: Microsoft ended support for Publisher this month, but users with orphaned documents still have options. Support for perpetual versions ended on October 13, but those copies will keep working without further security updates, bug fixes, or technical support. Publisher left Microsoft 365 subscriptions on October 1, although existing installations may remain accessible until removal updates arrive. Those start reaching Current Channel devices in mid-November and Monthly Enterprise Channel devices in early December. Microsoft first let users know in 2024 that the venerable application would be scrapped, and the Windows behemoth offered little comfort to those who needed it. Microsoft suggested Word and PowerPoint as alternatives, but neither directly opens Publisher's .pub files. The Document Foundation, the organization behind LibreOffice, was quick to point users toward LibreOffice Draw , which uses the libmspub library to import Publisher files and can save them in OpenDocument Format (ODF). Other alternatives aim to recreate more of the Publisher experience. Adam Anderly, founder of Texas-based Saint Systems, created PubKeep to replace Microsoft's application. PubKeep is proprietary, with no plans to open source the code. But it doesn't require a subscription: a one-time payment of $99 buys the application. The application runs on Windows or macOS, and a lightweight browser version is available. It looks a lot like Publisher, and can handle files from Publisher 2000 through 2021. Publisher 97 and 98 are also supported, but the files are sent to a conversion service (with the user's approval) to be converted to a newer format, so anybody worried about data leaving their local device should think carefully before opening those older files. Anderly told The Register that the project began after users expressed alarm about losing access to decades of files because of Microsoft's plans. The first challenge was the file format itself. He said: "Microsoft never published a spec for the .pub format. It did document some of the pieces Publisher is built on: the OLE compound file container, the document properties, and the Office Drawing records used for shapes and pictures. item.dc:creator: Richard Speed
item.content:encoded: Microsoft ended support for Publisher this month, but users with orphaned documents still have options. Support for perpetual versions ended on October 13, but those copies will keep working without further security updates, bug fixes, or technical support. Publisher left Microsoft 365 subscriptions on October 1, although existing installations may remain accessible until removal updates arrive. Those start reaching Current Channel devices in mid-November and Monthly Enterprise Channel devices in early December. Microsoft first let users know in 2024 that the venerable application would be scrapped, and the Windows behemoth offered little comfort to those who needed it. Microsoft suggested Word and PowerPoint as alternatives, but neither directly opens Publisher's .pub files. The Document Foundation, the organization behind LibreOffice, was quick to point users toward LibreOffice Draw , which uses the libmspub library to import Publisher files and can save them in OpenDocument Format (ODF). Other alternatives aim to recreate more of the Publisher experience. Adam Anderly, founder of Texas-based Saint Systems, created PubKeep to replace Microsoft's application. PubKeep is proprietary, with no plans to open source the code. But it doesn't require a subscription: a one-time payment of $99 buys the application. The application runs on Windows or macOS, and a lightweight browser version is available. It looks a lot like Publisher, and can handle files from Publisher 2000 through 2021. Publisher 97 and 98 are also supported, but the files are sent to a conversion service (with the user's approval) to be converted to a newer format, so anybody worried about data leaving their local device should think carefully before opening those older files. Anderly told The Register that the project began after users expressed alarm about losing access to decades of files because of Microsoft's plans. The first challenge was the file format itself. He said: "Microsoft never published a spec for the .pub format. It did document some of the pieces Publisher is built on: the OLE compound file container, the document properties, and the Office Drawing records used for shapes and pictures. For everything else, we used libmspub, the Document Liberation Project's open source parser behind LibreOffice's Publisher import, as a reference. "Our testing showed it had gaps, so we wrote our own engine in TypeScript. The same engine runs in the desktop app and in the browser. From there we built a test harness around Publisher itself. We assembled a corpus of real-world .pub files. An evaluation engine renders each file two ways, through Publisher's own PDF export and through our engine, and compares the output page by page, so every change we make is scored against Publisher." He added: "For the parts no one had documented, we made small, controlled changes to documents in Publisher and studied how the saved files changed. A licensed perpetual copy of Publisher on a Windows machine is the reference." Anderly emphasized: "We never decompiled or modified Publisher itself. Beyond Microsoft's published specs and libmspub, everything we learned came from the files and PDFs Publisher produces." We took a copy for a spin and it opened every .pub file we tried, although that was hardly an exhaustive compatibility test. Anderly said the company would rapidly address problems reported by users. Register readers will be unsurprised to know that Claude Code is involved, something that Anderly says makes responsive support possible, with agents reproducing problems and writing fixes. "Most issues are fixed the same day," said Anderly. "That leaves us time to answer every report and email personally." Although the code is proprietary, Anderly told us: "The .pubk format we save to is open, so anything you make in PubKeep isn't locked in the way .pub files were." PubKeep describes .pubk as a documented ZIP-based format containing JSON and images. That makes its contents inspectable, although it doesn't guarantee another application can reproduce the layout. For Publisher users seeking a familiar replacement, PubKeep offers another option. The $99 price includes a year of support. What's more striking is how quickly a relatively small team built something that reproduces much of Publisher's functionality. PubKeep is part of a broader reimplementation trend. Other projects are taking on applications that remain very much alive, including Word, Excel, and Photoshop. ®

item.title: Musk disputes NASA safety panel's lunar launch estimates
item.description: NASA's safety watchdog, the Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel (ASAP), had good news and bad news for the space agency, and SpaceX boss Elon Musk quickly disagreed with some of it. Musk disputed the reported suggestion that approximately 22 launches might be needed to support a landing by the Human Landing System (HLS) variant of Starship on the Moon. "That's way too high," Musk responded on X. "Actual number will be more like 6 to 8." The US lunar landers being developed for Artemis require refueling in space, meaning additional launches to deliver propellant before astronauts can head to the surface. During Apollo, a single Saturn V launch was enough to send a fully fueled Lunar Module to the Moon. The problem is demonstrating reliable transfers of cryogenic propellant between spacecraft at the scale these heavier, more complex landers require. Apollo's Lunar Module used hypergolic propellants instead. To date, SpaceX has managed one Starship test flight to orbit. Many more will undoubtedly follow, but if the launch figure cited by the panel is accurate, Musk's rocketeers face a challenging road ahead. Even with the rescoping that made Artemis III a low Earth orbit demonstration of lunar technologies from Blue Origin and SpaceX in 2027, the Artemis program remains ambitious, particularly considering the desire to get humans on the lunar surface before President Trump leaves office. ASAP praised Artemis II and NASA's new administrator, Jared Isaacman, but raised concerns about future access to low Earth orbit. SpaceX's plans to phase out Falcon rockets and Dragon spacecraft could complicate any extension of International Space Station (ISS) operations and the launch of its deorbit vehicle. Then there is Boeing's Calamity Capsule, Starliner. Last month, a possible uncrewed launch date around December 2026 was mooted , but the panel now puts the earliest possible launch in mid-January 2027, with the schedule still under review. An end to Dragon operations could leave Starliner as the only commercial option for getting astronauts to and from the ISS, not quite the redundancy NASA hoped for, and a stark reminder that commercial businesses aren't required to provide services indefinitely and can change direction when their contracts end. There is also only one US alternative to the cargo variant of Dragon: Northrop Grumman's Cygnus. An international cargo alternative is JAXA's HTV-X. Russia continues to carry crews on Soyuz spacecraft and cargo on Progress freighters, but NASA has long sought US alternatives. A written report is due early next year, doubtless with plenty of observations and recommendations. ®

item.title: Torvalds: AI is fine for competent devs, but spare us the 'drive-by' patches
item.description: Linus Torvalds is embracing AI to write Linux kernel code, and some people are having fits. He has a message for them. So do I. Roy Schestowitz, editor of Tux Machines, summed up his reaction to the news as " Linus Torvalds Turns to Slop . " In the podcast Pivot to AI , podcaster David Gerard agreed: "Linux kernel goes full AI slop code." Meanwhile, in the Tom's Hardware comments section, commenter "LordVile" wrote: " This is a publicity stunt from his AI overlords [The Linux Foundation] who pay his wage." They followed this by saying this is the "same reason he's flipped-flopped on AI." I've known Linus for a few decades, and I don't take his use of AI as evidence that he's suddenly abandoned his standards. And the very idea that he'd do anything he didn't want to do with Linux on behalf of the Linux Foundation, or anyone else, is ludicrous. I get it, though. There are reasons to be suspicious of AI. I've written about many of them. For instance, AI model collapse , which happens when AI engines learn from other AI models and their ties to the truth fray. It's a very real problem. Not, mind you, that LLMs find the grist for their answer mills from very reliable sources in the first place. Even when AI gets good data, as it does in programming, its owners pay little to no attention to the copyrights and licenses protecting the open source code it picked up its coding tricks from. As for paying for the information it runs on, please! The very idea that Big AI must pay writers, artists, you name it, for using their work is anathema to them. All that said, when it comes to programming, the ship has sailed. AI is becoming part of the programming toolkit, whether its critics like it or not. Why? Because while you still can't vibe code your way into delivering production-quality software, when someone who knows what they're doing, like Torvalds, uses AI, it can be very useful. Anyone who says otherwise is just making the same mistake the Luddites did. Who now, some of you may ask? They were textile workers who attacked machinery in the early 19th century in protest against changes threatening their wages and livelihoods. You may have noticed that while people still weave cloth by hand, industrial production is mechanized. The same is happening now with AI and programming. I think we're about halfway through the process, and by 2030 or so, people programming by "hand" will be about as common as weavers doing it by hand are today. In short, get over it. I don't love it, either. I write for a living, and my business is being crunched too. At least in programming, quality work still counts, no matter how it's done. With writing, though, true AI slop is increasingly the rule, not the exception. Back to Linux: at the Linux Kernel Maintainers Summit in Prague the other week, Sasha Levin, a Linux kernel developer, announced that the maintainers had decided to " deprecate the Assisted-by Tag ." That means you no longer need to say if you used AI in your code su
item.dc:creator: Steven J. Vaughan-Nichols
item.content:encoded: Linus Torvalds is embracing AI to write Linux kernel code, and some people are having fits. He has a message for them. So do I. Roy Schestowitz, editor of Tux Machines, summed up his reaction to the news as " Linus Torvalds Turns to Slop . " In the podcast Pivot to AI , podcaster David Gerard agreed: "Linux kernel goes full AI slop code." Meanwhile, in the Tom's Hardware comments section, commenter "LordVile" wrote: " This is a publicity stunt from his AI overlords [The Linux Foundation] who pay his wage." They followed this by saying this is the "same reason he's flipped-flopped on AI." I've known Linus for a few decades, and I don't take his use of AI as evidence that he's suddenly abandoned his standards. And the very idea that he'd do anything he didn't want to do with Linux on behalf of the Linux Foundation, or anyone else, is ludicrous. I get it, though. There are reasons to be suspicious of AI. I've written about many of them. For instance, AI model collapse , which happens when AI engines learn from other AI models and their ties to the truth fray. It's a very real problem. Not, mind you, that LLMs find the grist for their answer mills from very reliable sources in the first place. Even when AI gets good data, as it does in programming, its owners pay little to no attention to the copyrights and licenses protecting the open source code it picked up its coding tricks from. As for paying for the information it runs on, please! The very idea that Big AI must pay writers, artists, you name it, for using their work is anathema to them. All that said, when it comes to programming, the ship has sailed. AI is becoming part of the programming toolkit, whether its critics like it or not. Why? Because while you still can't vibe code your way into delivering production-quality software, when someone who knows what they're doing, like Torvalds, uses AI, it can be very useful. Anyone who says otherwise is just making the same mistake the Luddites did. Who now, some of you may ask? They were textile workers who attacked machinery in the early 19th century in protest against changes threatening their wages and livelihoods. You may have noticed that while people still weave cloth by hand, industrial production is mechanized. The same is happening now with AI and programming. I think we're about halfway through the process, and by 2030 or so, people programming by "hand" will be about as common as weavers doing it by hand are today. In short, get over it. I don't love it, either. I write for a living, and my business is being crunched too. At least in programming, quality work still counts, no matter how it's done. With writing, though, true AI slop is increasingly the rule, not the exception. Back to Linux: at the Linux Kernel Maintainers Summit in Prague the other week, Sasha Levin, a Linux kernel developer, announced that the maintainers had decided to " deprecate the Assisted-by Tag ." That means you no longer need to say if you used AI in your code submissions. That doesn't mean you can turn in slop, though. That code won't pass muster. As Torvalds told me in a note the other day: "I think the whole 'don't use AI for commit messages' kind of argument … Maybe it's well-intentioned, but I think it's entirely misguided. I really think we want competent people to use AI as a tool." Competent is the key word there. Torvalds also wrote: "The 'clueless people using AI' problem is different. I do think we want to discourage that. Not discourage the people who use AI and truly want to learn and truly want to become useful members of the kernel community – but discourage the drive-by patches, and discourage people who just want to feel like they sent a patch and never really wanted to become anything more. We all start clueless, but some people spend the time and effort to become something more." Exactly so. As Torvalds said at Open Source Summit Europe : "I think [vibe-coding is] a wonderful way to find joy in programming. It makes you feel like you're doing something relevant. It allows you, as a new programmer, to do things that you would otherwise have a really hard time with." He added: "I love the concept of AI as a gateway drug" to programming. Besides, AI has already proven very useful for improving Linux code. As long-term Linux kernel maintainer Greg Kroah-Hartman told me back in March: "Months ago, we were getting what we called 'AI slop,' AI-generated security reports that were obviously wrong or low quality." But then, "something happened a month ago, and the world switched. Now we have real reports ." It's not just Linux, he continued. "All open source projects have real reports that are made with AI, but they're good, and they're real." True, the maintainers are getting buried in good bug reports now, but as Kroah-Hartman and discussed in Prague, AI bug finders might eventually exhaust the readily discoverable problems, easing the pressure on maintainers. Another AI win is that you can use AI to reverse-engineer Windows drivers for Linux more easily. Christian F.K. Schaller, Red Hat's director of software engineering, created hw-harness while working on a Linux driver for a slide scanner. This open source project provides " tooling for working out how a piece of hardware behaves so that you can write a Linux driver for it." By automating some seriously slow, tedious ways of figuring out what a binary-only driver was doing with the hardware, Schaller has made building Linux drivers from Windows drivers much easier. I know, because I did this myself back in the mid-2000s, and those manual methods are still what people use today. This could go a long way toward fixing one of those lingering annoyances of the Linux desktop: poor or entirely missing hardware drivers. In the meantime, Torvalds told me: "Well, in all fairness, we do clearly have an 'AI problem.' Or rather, we have two independent AI problems: we have a large codebase that AI finds real bugs in, and that adds a lot of work on already fairly overworked maintainers. And then we have people who use AI to generate patches without actually understanding the code in question." He continued: "But I'd argue that these aren't problems with AI itself; they are just problems that are exposed by AI. They are very much both very real problems, and I understand that people can really come to dislike – and even hate – AI due to them, but I do think the underlying issue isn't AI itself." It's how people misuse AI. In the right hands, as the top Linux programmers are showing us, AI can be useful. ®

item.title: The young Americans choosing Y2K cars over shiny new SUVs: ‘I get so much crap from people’
item.description: People under 35 are hunting for no-frills rides they can pay for in cash and fix themselves – defying expectations to take on steep loans Jack Price joined the marines in fall 2021 knowing he would need a car to get around base and that he couldn’t afford a new one. A joyless, month-long search through dealer classifieds and Facebook Marketplace listings ended when his mother spotted a 2010 Volkswagen Jetta posted on her office listserv by a co-worker moving abroad. With just 60,000 miles (96,560km) on the meter, the car (a manual!) was mechanically sound, and the air conditioning, sunroof and Bluetooth radio worked too. At $6,000, it was a steal. Price paid in cash. Five years on, the Jetta, which he called the Pewter Pebble, is still carting him from A to B in unassuming style. “I’ve completely driven it into the ground,” says the 30-year-old, who lives in Los Angeles. “All over bases, cross-country a couple times, not really lovingly. I get so much crap from people, but not people my age.” Continue reading...

item.title: Ukraine learns to fight without Starlink as Musk plays politics with satellites
item.description: Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service has played a pivotal role in supporting Ukraine’s successful resistance to Russia’s full-scale invasion for years. But with Starlink having become increasingly unreliable due to Musk’s political inclinations and the latest surprise disruptions to service in Ukraine, the Ukrainians and Europe as a whole are now facing urgent questions about how to move forward without it. As the world’s largest communications satellite network, Starlink can typically support high-speed Internet and data streams for any user or vehicle equipped with a relatively compact Starlink terminal. This has enabled Ukraine to maintain vital communications for both civilian purposes and military operations—and has also expanded the Ukrainian military’s capability to remotely control or provide guidance to drones used in both air defense against Russian attacks and for striking back at Russian targets. “Starlink currently offers some of the best satellite coverage available, with virtually no competitors when you consider the combination of cost, availability, and ease of use,” according to the head of hardware R&D at the Ukrainian defense company BlueBird Tech , who provided comments to Ars anonymously for security reasons. “In practical terms, the main limitation is the need to position the antenna so it can receive signals from the satellites.” Read full article Comments

item.title: Review: Crystal Lake suffers a bit from its obsession with Pam Voorhees
item.description: Peacock series Crystal Lake doesn’t feel like a Friday the 13th movie when you first press play, even though it’s set up to be a prequel to the original film. (This review includes spoilers of the original Friday the 13th movie but avoids major Crystal Lake spoilers.) Instead, Crystal Lake strives to build a drama that’s half homage, half uncharted territory, while giving a long-awaited backstory to Pamela Voorhees. The original villain in the first film, Pam Voorhees, shocked audiences in 1980 by popping up out of nowhere in the midst of a brutal camp counselor killing spree, then confronting the final girl with a Norman Bates-like delivery of the movie’s chilling tagline, “Kill her, mommy,” using the voice of her drowned son, Jason. Betsy Palmer as Pam Voorhees in Friday the 13th . Credit: via Paramount Pictures Linda Cardellini as Pam Voorhees in Crystal Lake. Credit: via Peacock Although the hockey-masked killer, Jason Voorhees, became the horror icon at the center of the franchise, his mom, Pam, continued to fascinate fans, who knew very little about her. Beheaded in the first film after just 13 minutes onscreen, her spirit would occasionally appear in later films, but the original actor, Betsy Palmer, who portrayed Pam refused to return, largely because the character has no depth. Read full article Comments

item.title: Rocket Report: SpaceX says no thanks to military launches; Spanish rocket nearly ready
item.description: Welcome to Edition 9.16 of the Rocket Report! Lots of SpaceX-related news this week including a couple of Thursday shockers. In one story, the company told the US Space Force thanks, but no thanks after being offered three military launch contracts. Then, on the civil space side of things, SpaceX's Starship may required up to 22 refuelings to support a lunar landing, a NASA safety panel said. As always, we welcome reader submissions , and if you don't want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar. Miura 5 getting closer to launch . PLD Space says its Miura 5 rocket, due to undertake its inaugural launch next year, is nearing final integration, Aviation Week reports . The rocket is one of three Miura 5s the company has already manufactured, with the other two designed to qualify key system elements, CEO Raúl Torres said in an October 19 program update. PLD Space now targets a first flight of the small-lift vehicle before mid-2027. Read full article Comments

item.title: BOFH: I talked to Claude and he says you're an idiot
item.description: Working in the same place for what feels like millennia can have its benefits, however working for the same place for what seems like millennia carrying over all the benefits of your original contract can be even better than that. Some of those benefits are, admittedly, useless to me. I'm unlikely to avail myself of the Company-reimbursed landline (that all on-call personnel are entitled to), and I won't be needing the 2400bps modem or the VT100 for after hours support. It appears that we've been racking up two weeks a year to a point that I now have sufficient sick leave to safely get leprosy. Obviously, I'm not going to exercise that particular option, but both the PFY and I have been considering roads not taken in recent times... ... "Ahh... Just, um, following up on your recent, uh, illnesses." The Boss asks uneasily. "Oh yes?" I ask. "This, uh, acute bronchitis a few Fridays back." "Oh yeah, it was terrible," I lie. "Hacking cough, not pleasant at all. I was wheezing like a coal-fired Trabant." "And that particular illness lasted... a single day?" "Apparently," I say. "All good now though." "And Stephen. He had acute... otitis media around the same time." "The ear thing?" I respond. "Yes, apparently it really affected his balance." "Okay, fair enough. But then you had acute sinusitis on the Monday? And Stephen had asthma on the Tuesday?" "Yes, that sounds about right." I nod. "Then.. Back spasms for you last Friday and campylobacter for Stephen on Monday?" "I blame myself. I carried a large Vindaloo banquet for six back to work on the Wednesday night. The PFY took the leftovers back home for dinner following day. He's never been great with food hygiene." "And then I see fibromyalgia for you and food poisoning for Stephen?" "Yeah, like I said, he's not that great with food hygiene. He tends to follow the five minute rule." "Hmm. And is there any reason why you seem to be getting sick in... uh... alphabetical order?" the Boss asks. "It's as much a mystery to you as to me," I admit, making a mental note to vary things a bit. "Illness seems to be attracted to us like a hippy to a salt lamp." "And, uh, no medical certificate for any of these illnesses?" the Boss enquires. "I checked with Claude, and he told me that according to my contract I'd only need a med cert for a three-or-more-days illness." "You have been ill for more than three days. "And then I see fibromyalgia for you and food poisoning for Stephen?" "Yeah, like I said, he's not that great with food hygiene. He tends to follow the five minute rule." "Hmm. "Illness seems to be attracted to us like a hippy to a salt lamp." "And, uh, no medical certificate for any of these illnesses?" the Boss enquires. "I checked with Claude, and he told me that according to my contract I'd only need a med cert for a three-or-more-days illness." "You have been ill for more than three days. "And yet your eyesight was sufficient for you to type in questions to Claude?" the Boss asks, astutely. "Oh no, I spoke to Claude." It's a bit early to be calling check-mate at this stage, but I have to admit to feeling smug. "The actual wording of your contract indicates that the conditions can be varied by written notice," the Boss points out. "And I take it you've written a notice?" I ask, noticing a folded page in the Boss' hand. The Boss hands the paper to me, still warm from the printer. "You'll note that it's in writing, signed and dated," the Boss points out. item.title: Is a job guarantee the solution to mass AI unemployment?
item.description: An old idea springs anew as a chorus of influential voices predicts that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitude In a preface to his book Capitalism and Freedom, the American economist Milton Friedman famously observed that a crisis can propel once-fringe ideas into the political mainstream. “Only a crisis – actual or perceived – produces real change. When that crisis occurs, the actions that are taken depend on the ideas that are lying around,” he wrote. The job of intellectuals, thinktanks and economists, he argued, is to refine the quality of these ambient ideas, so that good ones are ready when disaster strikes. Continue reading...

item.title: UK threatens subsea cable saboteurs with 14 years behind bars
item.description: Britain is threatening subsea cable saboteurs with up to 14 years in prison and unlimited fines, having apparently decided that Victorian-era laws aren't quite up to the job of keeping Russian submarines away from critical infrastructure. The government on Thursday set out plans to overhaul legislation dating back to 1885 and introduce tougher penalties for damaging the underwater cables and pipelines that keep Britain's internet and energy supplies running. According to Whitehall, subsea cables carry around 99 percent of the UK's international data traffic, while underwater pipelines account for 74 percent of its gas supply. Yet much of this infrastructure is protected by laws written when the telegraph was cutting-edge technology. The Submarine Telegraph Act 1885 originally imposed a £100 maximum fine for damaging a cable through culpable negligence. That might have been a reasonable deterrent back then, but it's unlikely to give today's would-be saboteurs much pause. Under the proposals, those who intentionally damage critical subsea energy or telecoms infrastructure could face up to 14 years behind bars. The proposals also set tougher penalties, including unlimited fines, for reckless or negligent damage. Subsea telecoms operators would face new legal duties to identify and manage security risks, while ministers would gain powers to direct companies and cable repair providers to take action where necessary and proportionate to protect national security. The government also wants to regulate fiber-optic sensing technology, which uses subsea cables to detect activity at sea but could pose a security risk if sensitive data falls into hostile hands. Unsurprisingly, Russia features prominently in Whitehall's thinking. In April, British forces exposed a covert Russian submarine operation near critical undersea infrastructure. The operation reportedly involved an attack submarine acting as a decoy while two specialist vessels surveyed Britain's cable routes. "The threats we face have changed dramatically, with suspicious Russian activity around critical undersea infrastructure, yet some of the laws protecting these vital connections date back more than a century," said telecoms minister Ian Murray. The plans aren't entirely new. In May, the government announced its intention to toughen penalties and introduce security obligations for cable operators. Thursday's White Paper spells out the proposed penalties and how far ministers could go in directing operators to act. It also follows warnings from Parliament's Joint Committee on the National Security Strategy, which concluded last year that Britain was insufficiently prepared for a coordinated attack on its subsea infrastructure. MPs and peers warned that government assessments focused too heavily on individual cable failures, rather than what might happen if attackers simultaneously targeted connections to Europe and across the Atlantic. Russian submarines aren't responsible for every severed cable.

Thursday's White Paper spells out the proposed penalties and how far ministers could go in directing operators to act. It also follows warnings from Parliament's Joint Committee on the National Security Strategy, which concluded last year that Britain was insufficiently prepared for a coordinated attack on its subsea infrastructure. MPs and peers warned that government assessments focused too heavily on individual cable failures, rather than what might happen if attackers simultaneously targeted connections to Europe and across the Atlantic. Russian submarines aren't responsible for every severed cable. Fishing boats and ships dragging their anchors do most of the damage, accounting for up to 97 percent of faults, according to previous government estimates . And even when sabotage is suspected, catching those responsible is another matter. Britain already has laws allowing life sentences for serious acts of state-backed sabotage, but they're not much use if nobody can prove who did it. That's rather difficult when the crime scene is at the bottom of the sea. And it might prove equally difficult to extradite suspects from enemy nation states. None of this is law yet. The government has opened a 12-week consultation on the plans, after which ministers will decide how to proceed. Whether the threat of a lengthy prison sentence will trouble Russian submariners is debatable. Even so, after 140 years, Britain's subsea cable laws are finally getting dragged out of the Victorian era. ®

item.title: Beware the claw: Do you want to win the bunny or reboot Android?
item.description: Today's victim of the bork fairy is a claw machine that even Android seems to have rejected for its alleged unfairness. And Google, as we all know, is all about fairness. Eagle-eyed Register reader Scott spotted the stricken machine in an arcade adjacent to a roller rink, a place our reader visited with a friend and described as "something my currently bruised body reminds me I hadn't done for about 20 years." We assume they were talking about roller-skating, and not the exertions of accompanying their pal. The machine itself is a recent iteration of the infamous claw machine, which has spent a century emptying players' pockets in exchange for frustration and the very occasional reward of tat. Infamously, the devices are sometimes rigged so the claw's strength varies between turns, and in several parts of the world, gambling laws cover the machines. However, the only gambling to be done here is on whether or not Android will boot. Like so many players in the past, the machine has lost this bet, and an Android Recovery Console is on show. We're not sure who lennie022 is – perhaps a user or perhaps some corporate account – but the words "release-keys" probably don't belong on top of the device. They're unlikely to entice any everyday players to part with cash. The usual recovery menu is hidden thanks to the dimensions of the screen. If something like this comes up on a mobile device, the volume up and down buttons tend to be used for navigation. In this case, the joystick is presumably the only I/O method, and the selected option would be pot-luck. Which, we guess, is the whole point. More discreet is the screen below the machine which, rather than encourage a player to grip the sweaty handle, is now plaintively asking for some removable storage (we've seen enough electronic gizmos to know what those pictograms mean) on a blue background that would bring a tear to the eye of many a Microsoft engineer. In fact, something that looks a bit like a blue screen of death and a borked Android? Perhaps this combination would lure an engineer to the controls… Sure, there's no obvious place to stick removable storage or attach a keyboard. But a waggle of the joystick couldn't hurt, could it? Perhaps one more? Dammit. Now we're restarting Android, when all we wanted was that pink bunny. ®

item.title: Vendor-affiliated AI agent tech gets adopted by friendly, funded foundation
item.description: The Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) has been entrusted with stewardship of four additional AI projects in the hope of broadening the set of vendor-neutral tools for making AI agents. The AAIF was founded in December 2025 under the auspices of the Linux Foundation as a vendor-neutral organization for the benefit of AI companies more interested in riding a tide that lifts all boats than making waves. It launched with three projects under its supervision: Model Context Protocol (MCP), goose, and AGENTS.md. With the four new adoptees, there are now 10 projects sheltering under the AAIF's wings. The donor organizations – Alibaba, Anthropic, Hugging Face, and OpenAI – have handed over control of OpenSandbox, Agent Skills, OpenEnv, and Open Responses respectively. Each of these projects provides functions that developers of AI agents – which typically combine models, tools, and a task loop – may find helpful. And having a more or less agreed-upon blueprint for implementation tends to make deployment easier and more predictable, at least until your AI agent unexpectedly ransacks some third-party organization. OpenSandbox provides a way to constrain or sandbox the capabilities of AI agents using various client SDKs, tools, protocols, lifecycle hooks, container runtimes, and assorted in-sandbox execution components. Agent Skills outlines a format for text descriptions that guide AI agents through specified tasks more effectively. It provides context that helps agents accomplish their goals. "We’re committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral," said Anthropic, an AAIF co-founder, in a blog post . OpenEnv offers a containerized service for creating reinforcement learning environments that can be built without much trouble, can interoperate, and can scale to meet demanding testing. And Open Responses is an open API specification for building LLM interfaces that can work with different model providers. It standardizes common request and response formats, streaming events, and tool invocation patterns. The AAIF's nurturing of these technical specs has attracted considerable interest from companies convinced that there's a future in AI agents. The organization has surpassed 300 members in less than a year, with 60 coming on board this quarter, including Ant Group, Gates Foundation, MongoDB, Nutanix, Royal Bank of Canada, Vercel, and Vultr as Gold Members. This enthusiastic (or credulous) embrace of AI agents may be a bit too rapid for some industries. Axios is reporting that US banks have become concerned that AI agents are interacting with customer accounts without bank authorization (though not necessarily without customer authorization). ®

item.title: Apple Watch Ultra 4 review: longer battery life but still awaiting new features

That’s because several of the key features announced as part of Apple’s new smartwatch lineup for 2026 have yet to be enabled, awaiting updates towards the end of this year. That leaves the £749 (€899/$799/A$1,349) Apple Watch Ultra 4 the top dog, but basically the same as last year’s model .
